Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume Countable Choice. For a densely defined linear operator $T$ on $H$ the
adjoint $T^*$ is well defined and linear with linear domain $D(T^*)$; $T^*$ is
closed; for every $z\in\mathbb C$
$$\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\overline z),$$
and if $S\subseteq T$ and both are densely defined, then $T^*\subseteq S^*$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.
Then $T$ is closable if and only if $D(T^*)$ is dense in $H$. In that case
$\overline T=T^{**}$ and $T^*=\overline T^{\,*}$; moreover if $T\subseteq T^*$,
then $T$ is closable.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: [Well-definedness and density] $D_0$ is the linear span of the family and is a linear subspace; by [F1] the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique, so $S$ is well defined, and it is linear and maps $D_0$ into $H$. By [F1] the finite partial sums of the expansion of any $x\in H$ converge to $x$, so the span $D_0$ is dense in $H$.

[Symmetry and the series for $A$] Let $x=\sum_{n\in F}c_ne_n$ and $y=\sum_{m\in G}d_me_m$ lie in $D_0$, with $c_n=\langle x,e_n\rangle$ and $d_m=\langle y,e_m\rangle$ by [F1]. Then $\langle Sx,y\rangle=\sum_{n\in F}\lambda_nc_n\overline{d_n}=\sum_{n\in F}c_n\overline{\lambda_nd_n}=\langle x,Sy\rangle$ because $\lambda_n$ is real: $S$ is symmetric. For $x\in D(A)$ the sequence $(\lambda_n\langle x,e_n\rangle)_{n}$ is square summable with $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2<\infty$, so its finite partial sums are Cauchy: $\bigl\|\sum_{m\le M<N}\lambda_m\langle x,e_m\rangle e_m\bigr\|^2=\sum_{M<m\le N}\lambda_m^2|\langle x,e_m\rangle|^2\to0$ by [F1]; by completeness of $H$ the series $\sum_n\lambda_n\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n$ converges, its sum $Ax$ satisfies $\|Ax\|^2=\sum_n\lambda_n^2|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2$ (the finite-subset net of squared norms has the same supremum), and $A$ is linear because coefficient extraction is linear. If moreover $x\in D_0$, then $\langle x,e_n\rangle=0$ for all but finitely many $n$ and $Ax=Sx$; hence $S\subseteq A$.

[$S^*=A$] Let $y\in D(S^*)$ and $w:=S^*y$. For each $n$, $\lambda_n\overline{\langle y,e_n\rangle}=\langle Se_n,y\rangle=\langle e_n,w\rangle=\overline{\langle w,e_n\rangle}$, so $\lambda_n\langle y,e_n\rangle=\langle w,e_n\rangle$. By [F1] applied to $w$, $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|\langle y,e_n\rangle|^2=\sum_n|\langle w,e_n\rangle|^2=\|w\|^2<\infty$, so $y\in D(A)$; and $\sum_n\lambda_n\langle y,e_n\rangle e_n=\sum_n\langle w,e_n\rangle e_n=w$ by [F1], so $S^*y=Ay$. Hence $S^*\subseteq A$. Conversely let $y\in D(A)$ and $x=\sum_{n\in F}c_ne_n\in D_0$; then $\langle Sx,y\rangle=\sum_{n\in F}\lambda_nc_n\overline{\langle y,e_n\rangle}=\langle x,Ay\rangle$, so $x\mapsto\langle Sx,y\rangle$ is the restriction to the dense subspace $D_0$ of the bounded functional $\langle\,\cdot\,,Ay\rangle$ and is therefore bounded on $(D_0,\|\cdot\|)$; by [F2] $y\in D(S^*)$ and $S^*y=Ay$. Thus $S^*=A$.

[$A$ is self-adjoint] Let $z\in D(A^*)$ and $v:=A^*z$. For $y\in D(A)$ the pairing $\langle Ay,z\rangle=\sum_n\lambda_n\langle y,e_n\rangle\overline{\langle z,e_n\rangle}$ is absolutely convergent by [F4] and $\|Ay\|\,\|z\|$. Testing $y=e_m$ gives $\lambda_m\langle e_m,z\rangle=\langle Ae_m,z\rangle=\langle e_m,v\rangle$, that is $\lambda_m\langle z,e_m\rangle=\langle v,e_m\rangle$. By [F1], $\sum_m\lambda_m^2|\langle z,e_m\rangle|^2=\sum_m|\langle v,e_m\rangle|^2=\|v\|^2<\infty$, so $z\in D(A)$; and then $Az=\sum_m\lambda_m\langle z,e_m\rangle e_m=\sum_m\langle v,e_m\rangle e_m=v=A^*z$ by [F1]. Hence $D(A^*)\subseteq D(A)$; the reverse inclusion was proved in step 1.3 as $A\subseteq S^*$ with $S^*=A$, and directly: for $z\in D(A)$ and $y\in D(A)$, $\langle Ay,z\rangle=\sum_n\lambda_n\langle y,e_n\rangle\overline{\langle z,e_n\rangle}=\langle y,Az\rangle$ by absolute convergence and realness of $\lambda_n$, so $z\in D(A^*)$ with $A^*z=Az$. Therefore $A^*=A$.

[Graph core] Let $x\in D(A)$ and $x_N:=\sum_{n=0}^N\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n\in D_0\subseteq D(A)$. By [F1], $\|x-x_N\|^2=\sum_{n>N}|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2\to0$, and by step 1.2, $\|Ax-Ax_N\|^2=\sum_{n>N}\lambda_n^2|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2\to0$ because the series converges. Thus $(x_N,Ax_N)\to(x,Ax)$ in $H\oplus H$; since $x\in D(A)$ was arbitrary, $D_0$ is dense in $(D(A),\|\cdot\|_A)$, that is, $D_0$ is a core for $A$.

[Closure, essential self-adjointness and uniqueness] Since $S$ is symmetric, [F2] makes $S$ closable with symmetric closure $\overline S$, and [F3] gives $\overline S=S^{**}$. Since $A=S^*$ is the adjoint of a densely defined operator, $A$ is closed by [F2]; as $S\subseteq A$, the least closed extension satisfies $\overline S\subseteq A$. Conversely, for $x\in D(A)$ step 1.2 supplies $x_N\in D_0$ with $x_N\to x$ and $Sx_N=Ax_N\to Ax$, so $(x,Ax)\in\overline{\Gamma(S)}=\Gamma(\overline S)$ and $A\subseteq\overline S$. Hence $\overline S=A$, and $S$ is essentially self-adjoint because $\overline S=A$ is self-adjoint. If $T$ is any self-adjoint extension of $S$, then $T$ is closed and contains $\overline S=A$; since $A$ is self-adjoint and $A\subseteq T$ with $T$ symmetric, [F2] forces $T=A$. So $A$ is the unique self-adjoint extension of $S$.

[Positivity and eigenvalues] For $x\in D(A)$ the series $\sum_n\lambda_n|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2$ is absolutely convergent by [F4] and step 1.2: $\sum_n|\lambda_n||\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2\le(\sum_n\lambda_n^2|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2)^{1/2}(\sum_n|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2)^{1/2}<\infty$, and $\langle Ax,x\rangle=\sum_n\lambda_n|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2$ by continuity of the inner product in the first argument applied to the convergent series of step 1.2. Since the $\lambda_n$ are real the value is real, and $\lambda_n\ge c$ for all $n$ gives $\langle Ax,x\rangle\ge c\|x\|^2$ by [F1]. Finally $Ae_n=\lambda_ne_n$ directly from the definition of $A$ and [F1], so each $\lambda_n$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ with eigenvector $e_n\ne0$.

Step 1.2 proves A0=0 and the domain condition holds for x=0; step 2.1 includes the zero eigenvector case in the coefficient computation.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed every step 1.1–4.1 and exact operator/adjoint/Parseval/CS supplier definitions and statements. Real lambda is essential for symmetry; testing each basis vector gives both adjoint-domain inclusions. Weighted square summability proves convergence; both unweighted and weighted tails prove graph-core density and closure equality. Unique extension follows maximal symmetry. Zero lambda, repeated lambda and unbounded sequences are admissible; countable choice is explicitly carried from adjoint/Parseval suppliers. The stray reference to 1.2 instead of 2.2 in 3.1 and redundant assertion in 2.1 are immediately repaired by the explicit tail/direct pairing arguments already written; no fatal defect.

$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ ([[def-banach-space]], [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]) and let $A:D(A)\subseteq X\to X$ be a closed linear operator: $D(A)$ is a linear subspace and $\Gamma(A)=\{(x,Ax):x\in D(A)\}$ is closed in $X\times X$ with norm $\|(x,y)\|=\|x\|+\|y\|$. This extends the Hilbert-space vocabulary of [[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]] and [[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]] to Banach spaces. A scalar $\lambda\in\mathbb K$ belongs to the **resolvent set** $\rho(A)$ if $\lambda I-A:D(A)\to X$ is bijective and its inverse is bounded on $X$. Under Dependent Choice, boundedness of the inverse follows from bijectivity by [[thm-closed-graph-theorem]]; thus under DC this is equivalent to the bijectivity-only convention. For $\lambda\in\rho(A)$ the bounded operator $$R(\lambda,A):=(\lambda I-A)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(X)$$ is the **resolvent**, and $\sigma(A):=\mathbb K\setminus\rho(A)$ is the spectrum. One has $R(\lambda,A)X=D(A)$, $R(\lambda,A)(\lambda I-A)y=y$ for $y\in D(A)$, and $\lambda R(\lambda,A)x-x=AR(\lambda,A)x$ for $x\in X$; in particular $AR(\lambda,A)=\lambda R(\lambda,A)-I\in\mathcal B(X)$. This is the Banach-space form of the Hilbert-space vocabulary [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]; the shift convention $\lambda I-A$ is the same, with the closed graph theorem replacing the Hilbert-space bounded-inverse convention.

**Boundedness under DC.** Assume Dependent Choice. If $\lambda\in\mathbb K$ and $\lambda I-A$ is
bijective, then $\lambda I-A$ is a closed operator: its graph is the image of
the graph $\Gamma(A)\subseteq X\oplus X$ ([[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]])
under the homeomorphism $(y,z)\mapsto(y,\lambda y-z)$ of $X\oplus X$ with
inverse $(u,v)\mapsto(u,\lambda u-v)$. Hence $(\lambda I-A)^{-1}:X\to X$ has
closed graph and is everywhere defined, so the closed graph theorem
([[thm-closed-graph-theorem]], which assumes DC) makes it bounded; this is the
one place where an axiom beyond ZF enters, and it is the DC carried by the cited
theorem. The Banach-space vocabulary is [[def-banach-space]] with the scalar
convention of [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]; boundedness and
the space $\mathcal B(X)$ are those of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]].

**Elementary identities.** Let $\lambda\in\rho(A)$ and $R:=R(\lambda,A)$. Since
$R$ is the inverse of the bijection $\lambda I-A:D(A)\to X$, its range is
$D(A)$: $RX=D(A)$. It satisfies
$$R(\lambda I-A)y=y\quad(y\in D(A)),\qquad(\lambda I-A)Rx=x\quad(x\in X).$$
The first identity says $R(\lambda,A)(\lambda I-A)=I_{D(A)}$ and the second
says $(\lambda I-A)R(\lambda,A)=I_X$. Reading the second identity as
$\lambda Rx-ARx=x$ and rearranging gives
$$\lambda R(\lambda,A)x-x=AR(\lambda,A)x\qquad(x\in X),$$
that is $AR(\lambda,A)=\lambda R(\lambda,A)-I$ as everywhere-defined operators
$X\to X$; in particular $AR(\lambda,A)\in\mathcal B(X)$ even though $A$ itself
need not be bounded. The same identities hold for every $\lambda\in\rho(A)$,
and $\sigma(A):=\mathbb K\setminus\rho(A)$ collects the scalars for which
$\lambda I-A$ fails to be bijective or has an unbounded inverse. Under DC,
the latter possibility is excluded by the closed graph argument above. When $X$ is a Hilbert space this is the
Banach-space form of [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]],
with the same shift convention $\lambda I-A$; the closed graph theorem replaces
the Hilbert-space convention that the resolvent is bounded by definition.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: [Eigenvalues are spectral] By [F1], $Ae_n=\lambda_ne_n$ with $e_n\ne0$, so $\lambda_n$ is an eigenvalue of $A$. If $\lambda_n\in\rho(A)$, then $\lambda_nI-A$ is injective by [F2], contradicting $(\lambda_nI-A)e_n=0$. Hence $\{\lambda_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\subseteq\sigma(A)$.

[The resolvent outside the closure] Let $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $d=\inf_n|\lambda-\lambda_n|>0$, and define $Rx:=\sum_n(\lambda-\lambda_n)^{-1}\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n$ for $x\in H$. The series converges and $\|Rx\|^2=\sum_n|\lambda-\lambda_n|^{-2}|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2\le d^{-2}\|x\|^2$ by [F1], so $R\in\mathcal B(H)$ with $\|R\|\le d^{-1}$; testing on $e_n$ gives $\|R\|\ge\sup_n|\lambda-\lambda_n|^{-1}=d^{-1}$, so $\|R\|=d^{-1}$. For $x\in H$, the coefficients of $Rx$ satisfy $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|(\lambda-\lambda_n)^{-1}\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2\le(1+|\lambda|d^{-1})^2\sum_n|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2<\infty$ because $|\lambda_n|\le|\lambda-\lambda_n|+|\lambda|\le|\lambda-\lambda_n|(1+|\lambda|d^{-1})$ for every $n$; hence $Rx\in D(A)$ by [F1]. Computing coefficients with [F1] gives $(\lambda I-A)Rx=\sum_n\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n=x$, and symmetrically $R(\lambda I-A)x=\sum_n(\lambda-\lambda_n)^{-1}(\lambda-\lambda_n)\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n=x$ for $x\in D(A)$. So $\lambda I-A$ is bijective with bounded inverse $R$, that is, $\lambda\in\rho(A)$ and $R(\lambda,A)=R$ by [F2].

[Closure points are spectral] Let $\lambda\in\overline{\{\lambda_n\}}$. If $\lambda=\lambda_m$ for some $m$, then $\lambda\in\sigma(A)$ by step 1.1. Otherwise pick a subsequence with $\lambda_{n_k}\to\lambda$ and $\lambda_{n_k}\ne\lambda$ for all $k$, and suppose for contradiction that $\lambda\in\rho(A)$. Then $1=\|e_{n_k}\|=\|R(\lambda,A)(\lambda I-A)e_{n_k}\|=\|R(\lambda,A)(\lambda-\lambda_{n_k})e_{n_k}\|\le\|R(\lambda,A)\|\,|\lambda-\lambda_{n_k}|\to0$, which is impossible. Hence $\lambda\in\sigma(A)$.

[Conclusion] Steps 1.1 and 2.1 give $\overline{\{\lambda_n\}}\subseteq\sigma(A)$, and step 1.2 gives $\mathbb C\setminus\overline{\{\lambda_n\}}\subseteq\rho(A)$; taking complements yields $\sigma(A)\subseteq\overline{\{\lambda_n\}}$. Hence $\sigma(A)=\overline{\{\lambda_n\}}$, and the equivalence "$\lambda\in\rho(A)$ exactly when $\inf_n|\lambda-\lambda_n|>0$" together with the resolvent formula and its norm are exactly the contents of step 1.2. For (c), if $\lambda\in\sigma(A)\setminus\{\lambda_n\}$, the spectrum equality gives $\lambda\in\overline{\{\lambda_n\}}$, so a subsequence with $\lambda_{n_k}\to\lambda$ satisfies $\|(\lambda I-A)e_{n_k}\|=|\lambda-\lambda_{n_k}|\to0$ and $\|e_{n_k}\|=1$. If $x\in D(A)$ and $Ax=\lambda x$, then comparing coefficients in the complete orthonormal family gives $(\lambda_n-\lambda)\langle x,e_n\rangle=0$ for every $n$; because $\lambda\ne\lambda_n$, every coefficient vanishes, and Parseval gives $x=0$. Thus $\ker(\lambda I-A)=\{0\}$ and $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue. No further spectral-type classification is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A finite-valued function $f=u+iv:X\to\mathbb C$ is **measurable** when $u,v$ are real measurable functions. Write
$$N_p(f)=\begin{cases}\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty,\end{cases}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad N_\infty(f)=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty]:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}.$$
The finite case uses the real power; the infinite case is assigned directly,
so $N_p(f)$ is defined for every measurable finite-valued complex $f$.
The infimum of the empty set of finite bounds is $\infty$; equivalently allow $M=\infty$. Define $\mathcal L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\{f:f\text{ measurable},N_p(f)<\infty\}$ and its **set quotient** $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\mathcal L^p/\!\sim$, where $f\sim g$ means $f=g$ a.e. This extends [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]. Norm and vector-space assertions are established separately.

Here $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$ and $\overline{u+iv}=u-iv$ as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. These operations preserve measurability: $u^2+v^2$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and
$$\{|f|>a\}=\begin{cases}\{u^2+v^2>a^2\},&a\ge0,\\X,&a<0.\end{cases}$$
Thus [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]] applies. For $g=a+ib$, the formulas $fg=(ua-vb)+i(ub+va)$ and $\overline f=u-iv$ prove the remaining claims by real arithmetic closure. Nonnegative powers are measurable because $\{r^t>b\}=\{r>b^{1/t}\}$ for $r\ge0,t>0,b\ge0$, with the negative thresholds automatic.

A **finite simple** complex function has finite range and measurable fibers. Its **finite-measure support** condition is $\mu(\{s\ne0\})<\infty$. This concerns the nonzero set, not compactness of its closure. The zero function is an admissible finite simple function, including when $X=\varnothing$ or $\mu(X)=0$.

Integration is componentwise: for integrable $f=u+iv$,
$$\int f\,d\mu=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$
This is the earlier convention of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The inequalities $|u|,|v|\le|f|\le|u|+|v|$ show that integrability of the modulus and integrability of both components are equivalent.

For $n\ge1$, define complex $C_c(\mathbb R^n)$, $C_0(\mathbb R^n)$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ by requiring both components to lie in the corresponding real spaces ([[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]], [[def-c-zero-on-rn]]). Derivatives are componentwise, with the multi-index and all-ordered-partials conventions of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. The union of the two compact component supports is compact. A measurable complex $f$ is **locally integrable** for Lebesgue measure if $\int_K|f|<\infty$ on every compact $K$. The component inequalities give the equivalent componentwise condition. By [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], closed bounded balls are compact and each compact set is bounded. Hence compact integrability implies integrability on every bounded open ball by restriction from its closure; conversely each compact set is contained in a bounded open ball. These prove both directions of the ball formulation.

For a topological $X$ with Borel sets contained in $\mathcal A$, define
$$\operatorname{ess\,supp}_\mu f=X\setminus\bigcup\{U:U\text{ open and }f=0\text{ a.e. on }U\}.$$
Changing $f$ on one measurable null set preserves the zero-a.e. property on every $U$, since the union of that set and the old exceptional set is null. Thus essential support depends only on the a.e. class. Ordinary support means $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}$ and can change with the representative.

For the following illustration assume [[def-countable-choice]]. For $f=\mathbf1_{\mathbb Q}$ on $\mathbb R$, [[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]] gives $f=0$ Lebesgue-a.e.; therefore $N_\infty(f)=0$ and $\operatorname{ess\,supp}f=\varnothing$, since $U=\mathbb R$ occurs in the union. But [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]] gives $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}=\mathbb R$. For the Dirac probability measure at zero ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), the bound $1$ holds everywhere and every $0\le M<1$ fails on $\{0\}$, of measure one. Thus $N_{\infty,\delta_0}(f)=1$.

The raw $L^2$ pairing convention is $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$, linear in the first variable. Its integrability and class invariance are obligations of the later pairing items. **Bilinear tests** instead use $\int fs$, with no conjugation of $s$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.

derivations.claim: [The Gaussian moments and polynomial classes] If $p g_0=qg_0$ as $L^2$ classes, $(p-q)g_0$ is a continuous function that vanishes almost everywhere, hence vanishes everywhere; since $g_0>0$, $p=q$. Thus the representative used to define $Y$ and $\partial_y$ is unique, so these operators are well defined on $P$. By [F2], $\|g_0\|^2=\pi^{-1/2}\int e^{-y^2}d\lambda=\pi^{-1/2}\sqrt\pi=1$, so $g_0\in L^2$ and $\|g_0\|=1$. For $k\in\mathbb N$ and $y\in\mathbb R$, $|y^kg_0(y)|^2=\pi^{-1/2}y^{2k}e^{-y^2}\le\pi^{-1/2}2^kk!\,e^{-y^2/2}$ by [F3]; hence $\|y^kg_0\|^2\le\pi^{-1/2}2^kk!\sqrt{2\pi}<\infty$ by [F2], so $y^kg_0\in L^2$. Every $pg_0$ with $\deg p=m$ is a finite linear combination of $y^0g_0,\dots,y^mg_0$, so $pg_0\in L^2$: $P\subseteq L^2$ is a linear subspace.

[Invariance of $P$ and $ag_0=0$] For a complex polynomial $p=p_1+ip_2$ with real polynomials $p_1,p_2$, the real product and chain rules [F4] applied to $p_1g_0$ and $p_2g_0$ give $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$; $Y(pg_0)=(yp)g_0$ has polynomial factor $yp$. Thus both $Y$ and $\partial_y$, hence $a=(Y+\partial_y)/\sqrt2$ and $a^\dagger=(Y-\partial_y)/\sqrt2$, map $P$ into $P$. Since $g_0'=-yg_0$ by [F4], $(Y+\partial_y)g_0=yg_0+g_0'=0$, i.e. $ag_0=0$. All members of $P$ are represented by componentwise $C^\infty$ functions by [F4].

[Adjoint pairing] Let $\varphi,\psi\in P$. They are componentwise $C^\infty$ by [F4], and $\varphi'\overline\psi$ and $\varphi\overline{\psi'}$ are polynomial multiples of $e^{-y^2}$, hence absolutely integrable by [F2]. Their product $\varphi\overline\psi$ tends to zero at both ends by [F6]. Apply the whole-line complex integration-by-parts identity in [F6] to $u=\varphi$ and $v=\overline\psi$ to obtain $\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi'\overline\psi=-\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi\overline{\psi'}$. Therefore $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=2^{-1/2}\int(y\varphi-\varphi')\overline\psi=2^{-1/2}\int\varphi\overline{y\psi+\psi'}=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$, since $y$ is real and $\overline{\psi'}$ is the derivative of $\overline\psi$; the second identity follows by exchanging $\varphi$ and $\psi$ and conjugating.

[Rodrigues polynomials] Define $H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$; each $H_n$ is a polynomial because differentiating $e^{-y^2}$ produces $e^{-y^2}$ times a polynomial, and $H_0=1$, $H_1=2y$. Put $F_n:=e^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$, so $H_n=(-1)^nF_n$. By the product rule, $F_{n+1}=e^{y^2}\frac{d}{dy}\bigl(e^{-y^2}F_n\bigr)=-2yF_n+F_n'$, hence $H_{n+1}=2yH_n-H_n'$. We prove $H_n'=2nH_{n-1}$ for all $n\ge1$ by strong induction: for $n=1$ this is $H_1'=2=2H_0$, and $H_2=4y^2-2$ gives $H_2'=8y=4H_1$. For $n\ge2$, if it holds for all $1\le j\le n$, then differentiating the displayed relation at $n$ gives $H_{n+1}'=2H_n+2yH_n'-H_n''$, while the induction hypothesis gives $H_n'=2nH_{n-1}$ and $H_n''=2nH_{n-1}'=4n(n-1)H_{n-2}$, and the same relation at $n-1$ reads $H_n=2yH_{n-1}-H_{n-1}'$, so $2yH_{n-1}=H_n+2(n-1)H_{n-2}$; substituting, $H_{n+1}'=2H_n+2n\bigl(H_n+2(n-1)H_{n-2}\bigr)-4n(n-1)H_{n-2}=2(n+1)H_n$, which is the claim for $n+1$. Hence $H_n'=2nH_{n-1}$ for all $n\ge1$, and the displayed relation becomes the three-term recurrence $H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$. Induction on this recurrence gives that $H_n$ has degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$ (the term $2yH_n$ contributes $2\cdot2^n=2^{n+1}$ to $y^{n+1}$ and $-2nH_{n-1}$ only degree $n-1$) and that $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, true for $n=0,1$ and inherited.

[Commutator] On any $C^\infty$ function $\varphi$, $2(aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a)=(Y+\partial_y)(Y-\partial_y)-(Y-\partial_y)(Y+\partial_y)$, and expanding with the product rule [F4] gives $(Y+\partial_y)(Y-\partial_y)=Y^2-Y\partial_y+\partial_yY-\partial_y^2$ and $(Y-\partial_y)(Y+\partial_y)=Y^2+Y\partial_y-\partial_yY-\partial_y^2$; subtracting gives $2(\partial_yY-Y\partial_y)=2I$ because $\partial_y(Y\varphi)-Y(\partial_y\varphi)=\varphi$. [Identification of $g_n$] We prove $g_n=H_ng_0/\sqrt{2^nn!}$ by induction on $n$. For $n=0$ this is $g_0=H_0g_0$. Assume it holds for $n$; by step 1.2 and [F4], $(Y-\partial_y)(H_ng_0)=(2yH_n-H_n')g_0=H_{n+1}g_0$ by step 1.4, so $g_{n+1}=a^\dagger g_n/\sqrt{n+1}=(Y-\partial_y)H_ng_0/(\sqrt2\sqrt{n+1}\sqrt{2^nn!})=H_{n+1}g_0/\sqrt{2^{n+1}(n+1)!}$, which completes the induction.

[Ladder relations] From $[a,a^\dagger]=I$ on $P$ we prove $[a,(a^\dagger)^n]=n(a^\dagger)^{n-1}$ on $P$ for every $n\ge1$: for $n=1$ this is step 2.1, and if it holds for $n$ then $[a,(a^\dagger)^{n+1}]=[a,(a^\dagger)^n]a^\dagger+(a^\dagger)^n[a,a^\dagger]=n(a^\dagger)^{n-1}a^\dagger+(a^\dagger)^n=(n+1)(a^\dagger)^n$, all evaluated on $P$, which $(a^\dagger)^n$ and $a$ preserve by step 1.2. Since $ag_0=0$, for $n\ge1$ we get $ag_n=[a,(a^\dagger)^n]g_0/\sqrt{n!}=n(a^\dagger)^{n-1}g_0/\sqrt{n!}=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$, while $ag_0=0$; by definition $a^\dagger g_n=(a^\dagger)^{n+1}g_0/\sqrt{n!}=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$ for every $n$, hence $a^\dagger ag_n=\sqrt n\,a^\dagger g_{n-1}=ng_n$ and, using $aa^\dagger=a^\dagger a+I$ from step 2.1, $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$.

[The $y$ and $\partial_y$ actions] In the formulas containing $g_{n-1}$ at $n=0$, set $g_{-1}:=0$; this is the zero vector, so both formulas at $n=0$ are exactly the two ladder identities with $ag_0=0$. All identities are in $L^2$, where equalities mean equality of classes, and the underlying functions agree pointwise because both sides are represented by continuous functions; the polynomial identities of step 1.4 are pointwise identities of polynomials.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A finite-valued function $f=u+iv:X\to\mathbb C$ is **measurable** when $u,v$ are real measurable functions. Write
$$N_p(f)=\begin{cases}\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty,\end{cases}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad N_\infty(f)=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty]:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}.$$
The finite case uses the real power; the infinite case is assigned directly,
so $N_p(f)$ is defined for every measurable finite-valued complex $f$.
The infimum of the empty set of finite bounds is $\infty$; equivalently allow $M=\infty$. Define $\mathcal L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\{f:f\text{ measurable},N_p(f)<\infty\}$ and its **set quotient** $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\mathcal L^p/\!\sim$, where $f\sim g$ means $f=g$ a.e. This extends [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]. Norm and vector-space assertions are established separately.

Here $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$ and $\overline{u+iv}=u-iv$ as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. These operations preserve measurability: $u^2+v^2$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and
$$\{|f|>a\}=\begin{cases}\{u^2+v^2>a^2\},&a\ge0,\\X,&a<0.\end{cases}$$
Thus [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]] applies. For $g=a+ib$, the formulas $fg=(ua-vb)+i(ub+va)$ and $\overline f=u-iv$ prove the remaining claims by real arithmetic closure. Nonnegative powers are measurable because $\{r^t>b\}=\{r>b^{1/t}\}$ for $r\ge0,t>0,b\ge0$, with the negative thresholds automatic.

A **finite simple** complex function has finite range and measurable fibers. Its **finite-measure support** condition is $\mu(\{s\ne0\})<\infty$. This concerns the nonzero set, not compactness of its closure. The zero function is an admissible finite simple function, including when $X=\varnothing$ or $\mu(X)=0$.

Integration is componentwise: for integrable $f=u+iv$,
$$\int f\,d\mu=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$
This is the earlier convention of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The inequalities $|u|,|v|\le|f|\le|u|+|v|$ show that integrability of the modulus and integrability of both components are equivalent.

For $n\ge1$, define complex $C_c(\mathbb R^n)$, $C_0(\mathbb R^n)$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ by requiring both components to lie in the corresponding real spaces ([[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]], [[def-c-zero-on-rn]]). Derivatives are componentwise, with the multi-index and all-ordered-partials conventions of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. The union of the two compact component supports is compact. A measurable complex $f$ is **locally integrable** for Lebesgue measure if $\int_K|f|<\infty$ on every compact $K$. The component inequalities give the equivalent componentwise condition. By [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], closed bounded balls are compact and each compact set is bounded. Hence compact integrability implies integrability on every bounded open ball by restriction from its closure; conversely each compact set is contained in a bounded open ball. These prove both directions of the ball formulation.

For a topological $X$ with Borel sets contained in $\mathcal A$, define
$$\operatorname{ess\,supp}_\mu f=X\setminus\bigcup\{U:U\text{ open and }f=0\text{ a.e. on }U\}.$$
Changing $f$ on one measurable null set preserves the zero-a.e. property on every $U$, since the union of that set and the old exceptional set is null. Thus essential support depends only on the a.e. class. Ordinary support means $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}$ and can change with the representative.

derivations.claim: [Orthogonality] Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$. By [F2] with $\varphi=ag_n$ and $\psi=g_m$, $\langle a^\dagger ag_n,g_m\rangle=\langle ag_n,ag_m\rangle$; by [F2] with $\varphi=ag_m$ and $\psi=g_n$ and then conjugating, $\langle g_n,a^\dagger ag_m\rangle=\langle ag_n,ag_m\rangle$ as well. Using $a^\dagger ag_k=kg_k$ from [F1] on both sides, $n\langle g_n,g_m\rangle=m\langle g_n,g_m\rangle$. If $n=m$ this gives no information; if $n\ne m$ and $n,m\ge1$ it gives $\langle g_n,g_m\rangle=0$. If $m=0$ use $ag_0=0$: then $\langle ag_n,ag_0\rangle=0$, and the first identity reads $n\langle g_n,g_0\rangle=0$, so $\langle g_n,g_0\rangle=0$ for $n\ge1$; conjugate symmetry gives $\langle g_0,g_n\rangle=0$ as well.

[Eigenvalue equation] By [F4], $Y^2-\partial_y^2=2a^\dagger a+I$ on $P$. Evaluating at $g_n$ and using [F1] gives $(-\partial_y^2+Y^2)g_n=2ng_n+g_n=(2n+1)g_n$ as classes in $L^2$; the left side is computed on the smooth representative $g_n$, and the equality of classes holds because the two sides are continuous functions agreeing in $L^2$. The displayed form for $\varphi\in P$ with $Y^2\varphi=y^2\varphi$ is the same identity.

[Unit norms] $\|g_0\|=1$ by [F1]. For $n\ge0$, applying [F2] with $\varphi=g_n$, $\psi=a^\dagger g_n$ gives $\|a^\dagger g_n\|^2=\langle a^\dagger g_n,a^\dagger g_n\rangle=\langle g_n,aa^\dagger g_n\rangle=(n+1)\|g_n\|^2$ by $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$ from [F1]. Since $g_{n+1}=a^\dagger g_n/\sqrt{n+1}$ by [F1], $\|g_{n+1}\|^2=\|a^\dagger g_n\|^2/(n+1)=\|g_n\|^2$. Induction gives $\|g_n\|=1$ for every $n$. Together with step 1.1, $\langle g_n,g_m\rangle=\delta_{nm}$.

[Ladder pairings] For $n\ne m$, $\langle ag_n,ag_m\rangle=\sqrt{nm}\langle g_{n-1},g_{m-1}\rangle=0$ by step 2.1 when $n,m\ge1$, and $\langle ag_0,\cdot\rangle=0$; for $n=m$ it equals $n\|g_{n-1}\|^2=n$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product linear in the first argument, and let $g_0,P,a,a^\dagger,g_n$ and $H_n$ be as in [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]]. Then, for all $m,n\in\mathbb N$:

(a) $\langle g_n,g_m\rangle=\delta_{nm}$; in particular $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is an orthonormal family in $L^2$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]);

(b) the eigenvalue equation $(-\partial_y^2+Y^2)g_n=(2n+1)g_n$ holds as an identity of $L^2$ classes; more precisely $Y^2-\partial_y^2=2a^\dagger a+I$ as operators on $P$, so that on $P$

$$-\varphi''+y^2\varphi=2a^\dagger a\varphi+\varphi\qquad(\varphi\in P);$$

(c) $\langle ag_n,ag_m\rangle=n\,\delta_{nm}$ and $\langle a^\dagger g_n,a^\dagger g_m\rangle=(n+1)\delta_{nm}$ for all $n,m\in\mathbb N$.

No completeness of the family $(g_n)$ is asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. (c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.
Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ ([[def-series]]).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   ([[def-bounded-set]]), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

derivations.claim: [Reduction to the moment criterion] Since $(g_n)$ is orthonormal by [F1], [F2] reduces completeness to the statement that no nonzero $f\in L^2$ is orthogonal to every $g_n$; the expansion and Parseval identities are part of the same equivalence. The moment criterion (a) is proved first, and then applied.

[Vanishing moments] Let $f\in L^2$ satisfy the moment hypothesis of (a), and put $h:=fg_0$. By [F3], $h\in L^1$ and $\|h\|_1\le\|f\|_2$; every polynomial moment is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz because $qg_0\in L^2$ by [F1], and the hypothesis gives $\int hq=0$, in particular $\int h(y)y^jdy=0$ for every $j\ge0$. If instead $f$ is orthogonal to every $g_n$, then real-valuedness of $H_n$ and $g_0$ gives $0=\langle f,g_n\rangle=(2^nn!)^{-1/2}\int fH_ng_0$. The polynomials $H_0,\ldots,H_m$ have respective degrees $0,\ldots,m$ and nonzero leading coefficients, so successive subtraction of leading terms expresses every polynomial of degree at most $m$ as their linear combination. Thus orthogonality implies the moment hypothesis of (a). It remains to prove $h=0$ under that hypothesis.

[The transform vanishes] Fix $\xi\in\mathbb R$, write $w:=2\pi\xi y$ and $S_N(y):=\sum_{j=0}^N(-2\pi i\xi y)^j/j!$. Then $S_N(y)\to e^{-2\pi i\xi y}$ for every $y$ by [F5], and $|S_N(y)|\le\sum_{j=0}^N|2\pi\xi y|^j/j!\le e^{2\pi|\xi||y|}=:G(y)$ by [F5]. Moreover $hG\in L^1$: by [F3], $\int |h(y)|G(y)dy\le\|f\|_2\|g_0G\|_2=\|f\|_2\bigl(\int G(y)^2g_0(y)^2dy\bigr)^{1/2}$, and $G(y)^2g_0(y)^2=\pi^{-1/2}e^{4\pi|\xi||y|-y^2}\le\pi^{-1/2}e^{8\pi^2\xi^2}e^{-y^2/2}$ because $4\pi|\xi||y|-y^2\le8\pi^2\xi^2-|y|^2/2$; the last integral is finite by [F6]. Hence [F4] applies with $\widehat h(\xi)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\int hS_N=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j=0}^N\frac{(-2\pi i\xi)^j}{j!}\int h(y)y^jdy=0$, the first equality by dominated convergence, the interchange of the finite sum with the integral by linearity of the integral, and the final equality because all moments of $h$ vanish by step 1.2.

[Conclusion of (a) and (b)] Since $\widehat h=0$ identically, [F4] gives $h=fg_0=0$ a.e.; as $g_0(y)=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^2/2}>0$ for every $y$, $f=0$ a.e. This proves (a), and with step 1.1 it proves that $(g_n)$ is complete. By [F2] applied to the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$, every $f\in L^2$ has the stated expansion and Parseval identity, which is (b).

[Density of $P$] By [F2] and step 3.1 the closed linear span of $(g_n)$ is $L^2$. Since every $g_n\in P$ by [F1] and $P$ is a linear subspace, $P$ contains the span of the family; a subspace containing a dense subspace is dense, so $P$ is dense. This is (c).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A finite-valued function $f=u+iv:X\to\mathbb C$ is **measurable** when $u,v$ are real measurable functions. Write
$$N_p(f)=\begin{cases}\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty,\end{cases}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad N_\infty(f)=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty]:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}.$$
The finite case uses the real power; the infinite case is assigned directly,

$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.

arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the

   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable

claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis

derivations.claim: [$D$ is a bijective isometry] Define $D$ initially on a measurable representative $u$ of an $L^2(dy)$ class by the representative $\ell^{-1/2}u(x/\ell)$. With $T(x)=x/\ell$ in [F4], $\int h(x/\ell)dx=\ell\int h(y)dy$ for every $h\in L^1(\mathbb R)$. If $u,v$ represent the same class, apply this identity to $h=|u-v|^2\in L^1$: then $\|\ell^{-1/2}(u-v)(\cdot/\ell)\|_2^2=\|u-v\|_2^2=0$, so $D$ is independent of the representative. Applying the same change of variables to $|u|^2$ gives $\|Du\|^2=\ell^{-1}\int|u(x/\ell)|^2dx=\|u\|^2$; $D$ is linear, hence a linear isometry. The formula $D^{-1}v(y):=\ell^{1/2}v(\ell y)$ is also independent of representatives by the same change of variables, is linear, and satisfies $D(D^{-1}v)=v$ and $D^{-1}(Du)=u$ as $L^2$ classes. Thus $D$ is a bijective linear isometry.

[Transport of the orthonormal basis] By step 1.1 and the definition $\psi_n=Dg_n$, for all $m,n$ we have $\langle\psi_n,\psi_m\rangle_{L^2(dx)}=\int\ell^{-1}g_n(x/\ell)\overline{g_m(x/\ell)}dx=\int g_n(y)\overline{g_m(y)}dy=\delta_{nm}$ by the substitution of step 1.1 applied to $g_n\overline{g_m}\in L^1$ and [F1]. If $h\in L^2(dx)$ satisfies $\langle h,\psi_n\rangle=0$ for all $n$, then $\langle D^{-1}h,g_n\rangle=\langle h,\psi_n\rangle=0$ for all $n$ because $D$ is an isometry, so $D^{-1}h=0$ by completeness of $(g_n)$ and $h=0$. Hence $(\psi_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family.

[$H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the diagonal operator in the transported basis] Let $B$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(\psi_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n'=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)$, so $D(B)=\{f:\sum_n(\lambda_n')^2|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^2<\infty\}$ and $Bf=\sum_n\lambda_n'\langle f,\psi_n\rangle\psi_n$. By that lemma and [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]], $B$ is self-adjoint with $\sigma(B)=\overline{\{\lambda_n'\}}=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\}$ (a closed discrete set) and $\langle Bf,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ because $\lambda_n'\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}$. We claim $B=H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ as operators. First, $\langle f,\psi_n\rangle=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle$ by the isometry of step 1.1 applied to $f=D(D^{-1}f)$ and $\psi_n=Dg_n$; hence $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{f:D^{-1}f\in D(A)\}=D(B)$. Second, if $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and $c_n=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle$, then $D^{-1}f\in D(A)$ means $\sum_n(2n+1)^2|c_n|^2<\infty$, and the series $\sum_n(2n+1)c_ng_n$ converges in $L^2$ to $AD^{-1}f$ by [F2]; since $D$ is a bijective isometry it preserves limits of series, so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}D\bigl(\sum_n(2n+1)c_ng_n\bigr)=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n=Bf$, and $\sum_n(\lambda_n')^2|c_n|^2=\frac{\hbar^2\omega^2}{4}\sum_n(2n+1)^2|c_n|^2<\infty$. Hence $B=H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, giving self-adjointness, the eigenvalue formulas $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$, the spectrum, the domain formula, the ground energy $\hbar\omega/2$ and the lower bound.

[The differential expression on the core] For a polynomial $p$ put $F:=pg_0\in P$ and $f:=DF$, so $f(x)=\ell^{-1/2}p(x/\ell)g_0(x/\ell)$. By the chain rule and product rule [F5], $f$ is $C^\infty$ with $f'(x)=\ell^{-3/2}F'(x/\ell)$ and $f''(x)=\ell^{-5/2}F''(x/\ell)$. Since $\hbar^2/(2m\ell^2)=\hbar\omega/2$ and $m\omega^2\ell^2/2=\hbar\omega/2$ by $\ell^2=\hbar/(m\omega)$, for all $x$ one has $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f(x)=\ell^{-1/2}\bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m\ell^2}F''+\frac{m\omega^2\ell^2}{2}y^2F\bigr)\big|_{y=x/\ell}=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\ell^{-1/2}(-F''+y^2F)(x/\ell)$. By [F3], $-F''+y^2F=AF$ as functions on $\mathbb R$, because the operator identity on $P$ holds for the smooth representatives; hence the right side equals $\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}(DAF)(x)=H_{\mathrm{osc}}f(x)$ by step 3.1. This proves the pointwise identity. Moreover, if $\deg p\le m$, then $H_0,\dots,H_m$ have respective degrees $0,\dots,m$ and nonzero leading coefficients by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]]; triangular elimination shows that they span all polynomials of degree at most $m$. Since $g_n=H_ng_0/\sqrt{2^nn!}$, every $pg_0\in P$ is a finite linear combination of the $g_n$, and the reverse inclusion follows from $g_n\in P$. Thus $P=\operatorname{span}\{g_n\}$ and $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$. Since $P$ is a core for $A$ by [F2], its image under the unitary $D$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}DAD^{-1}$: for $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with $D^{-1}f\in D(A)$ choose $\varphi_k\in P$ with $\varphi_k\to D^{-1}f$ and $A\varphi_k\to AD^{-1}f$; then $D\varphi_k\to f$ and $H_{\mathrm{osc}}(D\varphi_k)=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}DA\varphi_k\to\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}DAD^{-1}f=H_{\mathrm{osc}}f$.

[Weak identity for general elements] Let $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$; put $S\varphi:=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi$, an element of $L^2(\mathbb R)$ by [F6]. By step 4.1 with the core $D(P)$, choose $f_k\in D(P)$ with $f_k\to f$ and $H_{\mathrm{osc}}f_k\to H_{\mathrm{osc}}f$ in $L^2$. For each $k$, write $f_k=DF$ with $F\in P$; by applying [F5] separately to the real and imaginary parts on $[-R,R]$, and using the fact that $F$ is a polynomial times $g_0$, whose products with $\varphi$ and their derivatives tend to $0$ at $\pm\infty$, integrating by parts twice gives $\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f_k''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f_k\bigr)\varphi\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f_k\bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi\bigr)dx$. By step 4.1 the left side is $\int(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f_k)\varphi$. Letting $k\to\infty$, [F6] and [F5] give $|\int(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f_k-H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)\varphi|\le\|H_{\mathrm{osc}}f_k-H_{\mathrm{osc}}f\|_2\|\varphi\|_2\to0$ and $|\int(f_k-f)S\varphi|\le\|f_k-f\|_2\|S\varphi\|_2\to0$, so the identity of the statement holds for $f$.

[Summary of the hypotheses used] The construction uses only the completeness of $(g_n)$ (step 2.1), the diagonal lemma and spectrum (step 3.1), the eigenvalue equation on $P$ (step 4.1) and the two integration-by-parts limits (step 5.1); no claim identifies $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with the domain of a maximal differential expression, and no physical meaning is attached to $m,\omega,\hbar$ or to $f$.
